name: The Molten Vigil

detectability.signature: A slow crimson heartbeat of thermal and radio emission, rising and falling on a metronome no one has explained.

proximity: Comm channels fill with rhythmic static synced to the Vigil's pulse
Ships feel gentle radiative heating, like standing near an open furnace door
contact: Plasma tongues lick across hulls at pulse peaks, scorching sensors and antennae
Shield generators strain to shed the surge load each cycle delivers
prolonged_exposure: Repeated thermal cycling fatigues hull plating to failure over days
Crew radiation loads accumulate toward mandatory withdrawal limits

phenomena: Visible plasma discharge arcs blooming in time with the pulse
Radiation spikes at irregular intervals riding atop the regular cycle
Electromagnetic interference patterns that repeat with eerie precision
hazards: Power system overload at pulse peaks
Radiation exposure exceeding safe limits during extended operations
opportunities: Energy harvesting potential: each pulse delivers harvestable charged matter
Strategic chokepoint control: the only clean approach lane to the inner system passes its fringe
known_incidents: Harvester platform Anvil Song rode out a mis-timed pulse in 2421; her crew survived in the shielded core, but the collection array was fused solid
description: The Molten Vigil is a small, disciplined storm: a knot of deep-red plasma half a tenth of an astronomical unit across that swells and dims on a strict six-hour cycle. At each pulse peak it blooms like a coal breathed upon, throwing arcs of crimson fire out along magnetic filaments. Between beats it settles into an ember-dark stillness that invites ships closer than wisdom allows.

The cycle has held for as long as instruments have watched it, though smaller radiation spikes scatter across it unpredictably, like spitting from burning wood. Harvesters time their runs to the troughs, skimming the charged matter the pulse throws outward before retreating ahead of the next beat. The platform Anvil Song learned the cost of a mistimed run when a spike arrived early and fused her entire collection array.

Stellar geologists date the storm to a supernova's incomplete aftermath some fifty-two million years ago, a scrap of stellar fury that never finished dispersing. Its perfect periodicity is what draws researchers, since no known plasma structure sustains such rhythm without a driving engine. Three survey stations have been built in its fringe; two were abandoned after spikes outran their shielding schedules.

Today the Vigil is worked like a tide: drone fleets sweep in on the troughs and the navy keeps a picket on the only safe approach lane through its fringe. Its rhythm is used as a sector-wide time standard, unofficially but universally. Newcomers are told the same thing the old harvester crews say: the Vigil always gives you six hours, and never gives you seven.
